patient.name: Callum Brennan
patient.complaint: Ten days of worsening headache and fever, now weak down his left side
background: Right ear pain and discharge for 3 weeks; one course of oral antibiotics from his GP
Witnessed seizure at home this morning
No past medical history, no regular medicines

Fevers and sweats; vomited twice today.

steps.lead: Callum has a **collection of pus** in his brain: the mass, the oedema and the raised pressure explain each of his symptoms.
Callum's source is his **ear**: otitis media spreading into the mastoid and on into the temporal lobe.

steps.q: Callum's weakness is on the left. Where is the lesion?

glossary.Brain abscess: A walled-off collection of pus inside the brain tissue.
glossary.Parenchyma: The functional tissue of an organ; in the brain, the neurons and glia rather than the coverings.
glossary.Streptococcus milleri: A group of streptococci (anginosus group) that classically form abscesses in the brain, liver and chest.
glossary.Ring-enhancing lesion: A lesion whose rim lights up with contrast on CT or MRI while the centre stays dark.
glossary.Mass effect: Pressure from a lesion pushing on and displacing nearby brain.
glossary.Midline shift: Displacement of the brain's midline structures to one side by a mass, a sign of dangerous pressure.
glossary.Vasogenic oedema: Brain swelling from fluid leaking out of damaged blood vessels into the surrounding tissue.
glossary.ICP: Intracranial pressure: the pressure inside the skull.
glossary.Papilloedema: Swelling of the optic disc caused by raised intracranial pressure.
glossary.GCS: Glasgow Coma Scale, a 3 to 15 score of eye, verbal and motor responses.
glossary.Contralateral: On the opposite side of the body to the lesion.
glossary.Hemiparesis: Weakness of one side of the body.
glossary.Oculomotor nerve palsy: Third nerve palsy: a 'down and out' eye, ptosis and a dilated pupil, a warning sign of herniation.
glossary.Mastoiditis: Infection spreading from the middle ear into the mastoid air cells behind the ear.
glossary.Sinusitis: Infection or inflammation of the paranasal sinuses.
glossary.Endocarditis: Infection of the heart valves that can throw infected emboli into the bloodstream.
glossary.Cyanotic congenital heart disease: Heart defects present from birth that shunt deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation, such as tetralogy of Fallot.
glossary.Tetralogy of Fallot: Congenital heart defect with a ventricular septal defect and right-to-left shunting, causing cyanosis.
glossary.Right-to-left shunt: Blood passing from the right heart to the left without going through the lungs.
glossary.Haematogenous spread: Spread of infection or cancer through the bloodstream.
glossary.Contiguous spread: Spread of infection directly from a neighbouring infected structure.
glossary.Septic emboli: Clumps of infected material carried in the bloodstream that lodge in distant vessels.
glossary.Cerebritis: Early, poorly defined inflammation of brain tissue before an abscess capsule forms.
glossary.Capsule: The fibrous wall that forms around a mature abscess.
glossary.Aspiration: Drawing pus out of the abscess with a needle, usually via a burr hole.
glossary.Burr hole: A small hole drilled in the skull to drain fluid or pus.
glossary.Ceftriaxone: An IV third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic that crosses into the brain well.
glossary.Anaerobes: Bacteria that grow without oxygen, common in ear, sinus and dental infections.
glossary.Neuro-observations: Regular checks of GCS, pupils, limb power and vital signs to detect neurological deterioration.
glossary.Coning: Herniation of the brainstem through the foramen magnum due to raised pressure, which can be fatal.
glossary.Lumbar puncture: Needle sampling of CSF from the lower back; dangerous when a mass lesion raises intracranial pressure.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein, a blood marker of inflammation and infection.

technique.stem: A 21 year old man has a 2 week history of worsening headache and fever. He had a painful discharging left ear a month ago. He is drowsy and has weakness of his right arm and leg. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. A contrast CT head shows a single ring-enhancing lesion in the left temporal lobe with surrounding oedema.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis: fever plus a focal lesion on CT.

clues: weakness of his right arm and leg
single ring-enhancing lesion in the left temporal lobe
steps.x: Subacute, febrile, ear source on the same side as the lesion, contralateral weakness, ring enhancement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Otogenic **brain abscess** in the left temporal lobe.

elim: Meningitis causes neck stiffness and photophobia, not a ring-enhancing mass.
Venous sinus thrombosis causes headache and venous infarcts, not a ring lesion.
Glioblastoma is not febrile and has no infective source.
SAH is a sudden thunderclap headache with blood on CT.

steps.x: **B. Brain abscess.** Rule: infection source + fever + ring-enhancing lesion = abscess.

technique.stem: A 44 year old woman has a 3 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the right frontal lobe on contrast CT after a week of fever, headache and personality change. She had sinusitis a month ago. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. Blood cultures are negative.
technique.q: Which investigation will give the definitive microbiological diagnosis?
o: Aspiration of the lesion for Gram stain and culture

steps.x: It asks for the definitive organism test, not the imaging.
An abscess has been found; cultures are negative, so you need the pus itself.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Aspirate the abscess** and send the pus.

elim: LP is dangerous with a mass and CSF is usually sterile.
Repeat blood cultures are often negative too.
Waiting a week delays treatment and still gives no organism.
Procalcitonin suggests bacterial infection but names no organism.

steps.x: **A. Aspiration.** Rule: gold standard = imaging + microbiology from drainage.

technique.stem: A 35 year old man has a 3.5 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left cerebellum with surrounding oedema on contrast CT. He had chronic otitis media. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg and GCS 14. Blood cultures have been taken.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Neurosurgical drainage with IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole

steps.x: Initial management of a confirmed abscess.
Large otogenic abscess, febrile, cultures done: treat now.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Drain it** and start **IV ceftriaxone plus metronidazole**.

elim: Steroids alone do not treat infection and may worsen it.
Aciclovir treats HSV encephalitis, not a bacterial abscess.
Oral antibiotics as an outpatient are unsafe for an intracranial abscess.
Radiotherapy is for metastases, not infection.

steps.x: **C. Drainage plus ceftriaxone and metronidazole.** Rule: drain and two IV antibiotics.

technique.stem: A 9 year old boy with uncorrected tetralogy of Fallot has a 5 day history of headache, vomiting and fever. He has a left hemiparesis. A contrast CT head shows a ring-enhancing lesion in the right parietal lobe. He has had no ear, sinus or dental infections.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which his heart condition predisposed to this lesion?
o: Bypass of the pulmonary capillary filter by right-to-left shunting
Direct spread from the middle ear
Reduced cerebral blood flow from heart failure

steps.x: A mechanism: how does cyanotic heart disease cause a brain abscess?

clues: no ear, sinus or dental infections
steps.x: No local source, so this is haematogenous spread through a right-to-left shunt.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The shunt lets septic emboli **bypass the lung filter**.

elim: The stem rules out an ear source.
Polycythaemia raises viscosity but is not the abscess mechanism.
Reduced flow causes infarcts, not abscesses.
Splenic dysfunction predisposes to encapsulated sepsis, not this.

steps.x: **A. Bypass of the pulmonary filter.** Rule: right-to-left shunt = emboli skip the lungs.

practice.stem: A 30 year old man has a 12 day history of headache, fever and two episodes of vomiting. He has had a discharging right ear for a month. He has left-sided weakness and bilateral papilloedema. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 130/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Subacute fever and headache, a chronic ear infection, contralateral weakness and papilloedema point to an otogenic brain abscess. Meningitis gives meningism rather than focal weakness.

steps.x: A diagnosis: febrile, focal and raised ICP.
Ear source, contralateral weakness, raised ICP, building over days, high WCC and CRP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Right temporal **brain abscess** from the ear.

elim: ADEM follows a viral illness or vaccine with multifocal white matter lesions.
Meningitis gives neck stiffness and photophobia, not a focal deficit with papilloedema.
Glioblastoma is not febrile and has no infective source.
HSV encephalitis gives confusion and temporal signs but no ear source or papilloedema.

steps.x: **C. Brain abscess.** Rule: ear infection + fever + focal signs = abscess.

practice.stem: A 10 year old boy with uncorrected cyanotic congenital heart disease has a 6 day history of headache and vomiting. He has a low-grade fever and a new right-sided weakness. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 110 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg and oxygen saturation 82% breathing air, which is his baseline.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Cyanotic heart disease with a right-to-left shunt predisposes to brain abscess; fever, headache, vomiting and focal weakness fit. Endocarditis is a source, but does not itself explain the focal deficit.

steps.x: A diagnosis in a cyanotic child with focal signs.
Right-to-left shunt, subacute, febrile, focal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Brain abscess**.

elim: Venous sinus thrombosis is possible with polycythaemia but less likely with fever and a subacute focal deficit.
Endocarditis is a source, not the cause of a focal neurological deficit here.
Medulloblastoma is cerebellar (ataxia), afebrile and slower.
Viral meningitis does not cause focal weakness.

steps.x: **A. Brain abscess.** Rule: cyanotic heart disease + focal signs + fever = abscess.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman has a ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe after recent dental extraction. Aspirated pus grows Gram-positive cocci in chains that form abscesses. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Streptococcus milleri (anginosus group) is the classic abscess-forming streptococcus, often from dental or sinus sources. The others are meningitis organisms.

steps.x: Organism question for a brain abscess.
Dental source, Gram-positive chains = streptococci; abscess former.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Streptococcus milleri**.

elim: E. coli is Gram-negative; neonatal meningitis.
H. influenzae is a Gram-negative coccobacillus.
Listeria is a Gram-positive rod, in elderly, pregnant or immunosuppressed meningitis.
N. meningitidis is a Gram-negative diplococcus causing meningitis.

steps.x: **E. Streptococcus milleri.** Rule: 'abscess' + streptococcus = milleri.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has a 10 day history of frontal headache, fever and behavioural change. Three weeks ago she had facial pain and purulent nasal discharge that was not treated. A contrast CT shows a ring-enhancing lesion in the right frontal lobe. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely source of the infection?
practice.e: Facial pain and purulent nasal discharge are sinusitis, which spreads directly to the frontal lobe. Mastoiditis spreads to the temporal lobe or cerebellum.

steps.x: The source of a brain abscess: match it to the lobe.

clues: facial pain and purulent nasal discharge
steps.x: Untreated sinusitis, then a frontal lobe abscess next door.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Contiguous spread from **frontal sinusitis**.

elim: Endocarditis gives multiple emboli and a murmur; none here.
Mastoiditis causes temporal or cerebellar abscesses.
Otitis externa is superficial and rarely spreads intracranially.
UTI is not a recognised brain abscess source.

steps.x: **B. Frontal sinusitis.** Rule: sinus = frontal; ear = temporal or cerebellum.

practice.stem: A 33 year old man has a contrast CT showing a 3 cm ring-enhancing abscess in the right temporal lobe with surrounding oedema, after untreated right mastoiditis. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 136/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on neurological examination?
o: Right lower motor neurone facial palsy
practice.e: A right hemisphere mass with oedema compresses motor pathways, so weakness is contralateral: left-sided hemiparesis.

steps.x: Examination finding: which side, and which pattern?
Right-sided lesion with mass effect.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Contralateral** (left) hemiparesis.

elim: Bilateral leg weakness suggests a spinal cord lesion.
Meningism is usually absent with a parenchymal abscess.
An LMN facial palsy comes from the nerve itself, not a temporal lobe mass.
Right-sided weakness would need a left hemisphere lesion.

steps.x: **B. Left-sided hemiparesis.** Rule: hemiparesis is contralateral to the lesion.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man who injects heroin is on IV antibiotics for tricuspid and mitral valve endocarditis. He has a new seizure and left arm weakness. A contrast CT head shows a ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema in the right frontal lobe. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Endocarditis seeds septic emboli by haematogenous spread; fever, seizure, focal weakness and a ring-enhancing lesion are a brain abscess. A stroke would not ring-enhance.

steps.x: A diagnosis in a patient with an infective source in the blood.
Bacteraemia, then a febrile focal lesion with a ring.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Haematogenous **brain abscess**.

elim: Meningitis does not give a ring-enhancing parenchymal lesion.
No known cancer; fever and bacteraemia point to infection.
An embolic infarct is wedge-shaped and does not ring-enhance.
A bleed is hyperdense on plain CT, not ring-enhancing with fever.

steps.x: **B. Brain abscess.** Rule: endocarditis + ring lesion + fever = abscess.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman has a 9 day history of headache and fever after a dental abscess. She has right arm weakness and papilloedema. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg and GCS 14.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Fever, focal weakness and papilloedema suggest a brain abscess: image first with contrast CT (or urgent MRI). Lumbar puncture is contraindicated with raised ICP.

steps.x: Initial investigation in a febrile patient with focal signs.
Possible mass lesion with raised ICP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Contrast-enhanced CT head**.

elim: EEG does not show a structural lesion.
LP with papilloedema and focal signs risks coning.
Skull X-ray cannot see brain tissue.
Echo looks for endocarditis later; the source here is dental.

steps.x: **A. CT head with contrast.** Rule: focal signs + papilloedema = scan before LP.

practice.stem: A 50 year old man has a ring-enhancing lesion in the left parietal lobe. He has no ear, sinus or dental symptoms. He has a new pansystolic murmur and splinter haemorrhages. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the source?
practice.e: A new murmur and splinter haemorrhages suggest endocarditis seeding the abscess: take blood cultures (with echocardiography). LP is unsafe with a mass lesion.

steps.x: Looking for the source of a confirmed abscess.

clues: no ear, sinus or dental symptoms
steps.x: No local source; signs of endocarditis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Blood cultures** for endocarditis.

elim: Abdominal ultrasound does not look for endocarditis.
Colonoscopy has no role here.
LP is contraindicated with a mass lesion.
Urine is not the source suggested by the murmur.

steps.x: **B. Blood cultures.** Rule: second-line tests look for the source, e.g. endocarditis.

practice.stem: A 31 year old man has a 2.5 cm ring-enhancing right temporal abscess after chronic otitis media. Neurosurgery plan aspiration today. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 130/82 mmHg and GCS 15. Blood cultures have been taken.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
practice.e: First-line empirical treatment is an IV third-generation cephalosporin plus metronidazole, covering streptococci and anaerobes. Oral antibiotics do not achieve adequate brain levels.

steps.x: Empirical antibiotics for a brain abscess.
Otogenic abscess: streptococci plus anaerobes likely.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV ceftriaxone plus metronidazole**.

elim: Aciclovir treats HSV encephalitis.
Benzylpenicillin alone misses anaerobes and some streptococci.
Oral amoxicillin is inadequate for an intracranial abscess.
Flucloxacillin is for staphylococcal skin infection, and oral.

steps.x: **C. IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole.** Rule: cephalosporin + metronidazole.

practice.stem: A 42 year old woman has a contrast CT showing a 3 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe with oedema and 5 mm midline shift. She had sinusitis a month ago. IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole have been started. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 132/84 mmHg and GCS 14.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: A large abscess with midline shift needs urgent neurosurgical drainage alongside IV antibiotics: it decompresses the lesion and gives the organism.

steps.x: Antibiotics are running; what comes next?

clues: IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole have been started
steps.x: A large abscess with mass effect: antibiotics alone are not enough.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent neurosurgical drainage**.

elim: Oral antibiotics at home are unsafe for an intracranial abscess.
LP risks coning with midline shift.
This is a treatable infection, not a palliative situation.
Radiosurgery is for metastases, not abscesses.

steps.x: **E. Urgent neurosurgical drainage.** Rule: drainage + IV antibiotics.

practice.stem: A 28 year old man with a known right temporal brain abscess, awaiting neurosurgical drainage, has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure on the ward that has lasted 6 minutes. He has IV access. His pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 150/92 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% on 15 L/min oxygen.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
practice.e: Seizures in a brain abscess are treated as they occur: a seizure over 5 minutes with IV access needs IV lorazepam. Oral drugs cannot be given during a seizure.

steps.x: Immediate management of a seizure in a brain abscess patient.
Over 5 minutes = treat now; IV route available; glucose normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV lorazepam**.

elim: Mannitol lowers ICP but does not stop a seizure.
LP is contraindicated with a mass lesion.
Oral drugs cannot be swallowed during a seizure.
Imaging can follow once the seizure stops.

steps.x: **A. IV lorazepam.** Rule: in an abscess emergency, control seizures, then escalate to neurosurgery.

practice.stem: A 36 year old man has a 3 week history of headache and fever after mastoiditis. A contrast CT head shows a lesion in the right temporal lobe with a thin bright rim and a dark centre, surrounded by low-density oedema. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which best explains the appearance of the lesion?
o: Enhancing fibrous capsule around a necrotic centre
practice.e: A mature abscess has a vascular fibrous capsule that takes up contrast, around a necrotic pus-filled centre that does not: the ring-enhancing appearance.

steps.x: A mechanism: why is it a ring?

clues: thin bright rim and a dark centre
steps.x: Weeks in: a mature abscess with a capsule.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **capsule** enhances; the **pus** does not.

elim: Fresh blood is bright throughout on plain CT, not a ring.
Calcification is not the cause of contrast enhancement in an abscess.
Venous infarction is not a rim-enhancing cavity.
Ventricular dilatation is hydrocephalus, not a lobar lesion.

steps.x: **D. Enhancing capsule around a necrotic centre.** Rule: cerebritis then capsule = ring.
